facts.text: Built between 1905 and 1907 as a brick school faced with granite in the Colonial Revival style.
An eight-bay addition was built between 1913 and 1914.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
Built in 1927 and 1928 in the Late Gothic Revival style.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places on November 18, 1988.
Stands in the Fishtown area of Philadelphia.
Designed by chief engineer John A. Wilson and built by Thomas Seabrook.
Stone arch bridge with a longest span of 103 feet.
Appears in Thomas Eakins's painting Max Schmitt in a Single Scull (1871).

name: Philadelphia High School for the Creative and Performing Arts

facts.text: Founded in 1978 by John R. Vannoni as a district magnet school.
Occupies the former Ridgway Library, built 1873 to 1878 by architect Addison Hutton.
Library building was adapted as a high school in 1997 by Kise, Straw and Kolodner.

name: Philadelphia Job Corps Life Science Institute

facts.text: Dedicated June 22, 2002 and rededicated on May 28, 2007.
Commemorates 610 servicemen from the Philadelphia area who died in the Korean War.
Features four black granite pillars listing casualties from each year of the war, 1950 to 1953.
Owned by the city and leased to the nonprofit Friends of the Philadelphia Korean War Memorial.
Dedicated in 1987 at Penn's Landing.
Lists the names of 648 Philadelphia servicemen killed or missing in action in the Vietnam War.
Designed by architect Perry M. Morgan, selected in 1985.
Amphitheater of polished charcoal grey Minnesota granite with ten panels depicting scenes of the war.
Site where President George Washington lived while Philadelphia was the capital.
Washington's household included nine enslaved people, whose names are memorialized at the site.
Designed by Irwin T. Catharine and built between 1928 and 1929.
Three-story brick building in the Late Gothic Revival style with a Tudor arch entryway.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
Stands in West Fairmount Park.
Land was bought by yeoman William Couch in 1718 and the house was likely built between 1752 and 1762.
Leased to the Cancer Support Community Greater Philadelphia through the Fairmount Park Conservancy.

name: Robert N.C. Nix, Sr. Federal Building

facts.text: Renamed in December 1985 for Robert N. C. Nix Sr., the first African-American congressman from Pennsylvania.
Features sculptures and reliefs by Donald De Lue and Edmond Amateis.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places on October 19, 1990.
Built between 1900 and 1901 in the Strawberry Mansion neighborhood.
Named for merchant Rudolph Walton (1826 to 1900).
Added to the National Register of Historic Places on December 4, 1986.
First service held on September 4, 1761 in Society Hill.
Land was donated in 1757 by Thomas and Richard Penn, sons of William Penn.
Shared a vestry and clergy with Christ Church until the two formally separated in 1832.
Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1996.

name: Second Bank of the United States

facts.text: Facades have eight Doric columns, and the design is based on the Parthenon.
Houses a permanent portrait gallery of over 150 founders' portraits, with over 100 by Charles Willson Peale.
Bank was authorized from 1816 to 1836 and the building is part of Independence National Historical Park.
Created in 1926 by Alexander Stirling Calder and installed in 1928 in Logan Square.
Depicts two figures representing Comedy and Tragedy.
Relocated in 1953 because of expressway construction.
Maintained by the Association for Public Art.
Built from 1897 to 1912 as a Civil War monument and gateway to West Fairmount Park.
Funded by a $500,000 bequest from type founder Richard A. Smith.
Adorned with 13 portrait sculptures, including equestrian statues of McClellan and Hancock.
Designed by Henry deCoursey Richards and built between 1909 and 1911.
Three-story granite-faced reinforced concrete building in the Tudor Revival style.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1986.
Opened in 1808 and built by Bishop & Sparks to produce lead shot.
One of the first lead shot towers in the United States.
The city bought the site in 1913 and turned the grounds into a playground.
Described as the oldest Methodist church in continuous use in the United States.
Congregation was founded in 1767 and moved into the current building in 1769.
Building was originally the William Henry Harrison School, in the Yorktown neighborhood.
Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1988.
Federal style mansion built in 1797 in West Fairmount Park by Samuel Breck.
Named for the roses that grew on the property.
Became part of the park in 1869 and is headquarters of the Modern Club of Philadelphia.
Georgian country house in East Fairmount Park built by merchant Joshua Fisher.
Owned by the Fisher family until the city bought it in 1868.
Destroyed by an arsonist on February 22, 1986, leaving the masonry walls and chimneys.
